children.text: A beach town tucked away at the southwestern tip of Negros Island, with the fine sand of Sugar Beach and Punta Ballo, sunsets over the Sulu Sea, and more than 40 dive sites. The journey there is long, but it rewards you with a quiet, unspoiled stretch of Philippine sea.

Sipalay is a coastal town at the southwestern tip of Negros Occidental, facing the Sulu Sea. It once thrived as a copper mining town, but since the mine's decline it has quietly built a reputation for its beaches and diving. Unlike Boracay, there are no large resorts or busy strips here — its biggest appeal is being an 'in-the-know' beach, with a handful of simple bungalows and dive shops gathered beneath the shade of palm trees.
There are two main beaches. Punta Ballo Beach, about
7km

south of town, is a small bay lined with dive resorts, where you can snorkel right in front of the beach. Sugar Beach, in front of Nauhang village north of town, is a stretch of sugar-colored, light brown sand about
1km

long, originally called Langub Beach. The road doesn't reach the beach, so you have to go in by small boat, which means there is almost no car noise. Both beaches face west, so at dusk the whole sea turns orange.

The underwater world exceeds expectations too. More than 40 known dive sites lie off Sipalay's coast, ranging from coral walls to artificial reefs and wreck sites. Water temperatures stay warm year-round at 27–30°C, and beginners can take Open Water certification courses at the dive shops in Punta Ballo. Even without diving, you can spend a day island-hopping around Campomanes Bay and the surrounding deserted islands.
It's a long haul —
4–6 hours

by bus from Bacolod or Dumaguete — which can be a burden for travelers with a short schedule. But it suits those who want to spend several unhurried days reading on the beach and diving, free of crowds and touts, as well as backpackers making a loop around Negros Island.
Sipalay became a city on
March 31, 2001
. As of
it has a population of about 73,800, an area of about 380 km², and 17 barangays. The copper mine, which had operated in the San Jose area since
, closed in
July 2001
amid labor disputes and environmental pollution problems, and more than 5,000 miners lost their jobs. Old ore-processing facilities remain at the mine site. The average annual temperature is about
and annual rainfall is about 1,945mm, and in late March the city comes alive with its cityhood anniversary and annual festival.

blocks.title: Watch the sunset at Sugar Beach

children.text: Sugar Beach faces west, so the sun drops into the Sulu Sea around
. Sit on the sand at a beach bar with a bottle of San Miguel in front of you, and you'll instantly understand why you came to Sipalay.
Book a boat dive with a Punta Ballo dive shop and you can explore coral walls, artificial reefs, and wreck sites. You'll often encounter turtles, nudibranchs, and lionfish.
Tour Campomanes Bay, a natural harbor ringed by mountains, by bangka boat, stopping at hidden beaches and snorkeling spots. The water is as calm as a lake, so even beginners can swim comfortably.
The coral area right off Punta Ballo Beach lets you see tropical fish even by wading in on foot. At low tide, wear aqua shoes so you don't step on sea urchins or coral.

blocks.title: Kayaking and a bridge walk at Tinagong Dagat

children.text: Tinagong Dagat, meaning 'hidden sea,' is a calm, emerald-green stretch of water in Barangay 4 (Latasan) in town, dotted with forest-covered limestone islands linked by bamboo bridges. Admission is about
per person; you can rent a kayak or paddleboard or tour it on a bangka hopping trip, and lodging and a restaurant are run on site as well.
Danjugan Island, about
3km

off the Cauayan Bulata coast, is a wildlife and marine reserve of about 43 hectares with five lagoons, a bat cave, and mangrove and limestone forest, managed by a private foundation, PRRCFI. Visitor numbers are limited, so you must book in advance on the official website. The
3 hours
tour costs about
per person and the full-day tour (lunch included) about
. Prices may change, so check on the
official website
Buy fish and squid at Sipalay's public market and ask your accommodation's kitchen or a restaurant to cook it for you — an inexpensive way to enjoy fresh seafood.

long), sunk by a Japanese air raid on
December 28, 1941
, lies at a depth of

It takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD) and about
40 minutes
from Cebu. Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and AirAsia operate several flights a day, with one-way fares of about
depending on the season. You can also use Dumaguete Airport (DGT), but there are few buses from Dumaguete to Sipalay.
From Bacolod Airport, take a shuttle van or taxi for about
40 minutes

to the South Bus Terminal in the city, then board a Ceres (Vallacar Transit) bus. Take a bus going directly to Sipalay or to Hinoba-an and get off at Sipalay. There are several departures a day, but timetables differ by route (via Don Salvador Benedicto, via Candoni, and so on), and accounts conflict on the first bus (early morning) and the last bus (around 6:40 PM), so it is safest to check at the terminal the day before and take a morning bus. The trip takes about
5–6 hours
, and fares are about
for an ordinary bus and about
for an air-conditioned one.
From the Sipalay bus stop to Punta Ballo is about
20 minutes
by tricycle, about
per person. There is no road to Sugar Beach, so from the Gil Montilla junction near city hall, take a tricycle about
15 minutes
(about
) to the river mouth at Nauhang village and cross by small boat (about
per person), or hire a boat to take you directly to your resort (about
). There is also a route by bangka from Poblacion Beach that takes about
15 minutes
. Many places will send a pickup boat if you tell them your arrival time in advance.
It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
by air from Manila to Dumaguete (DGT). From the Ceres terminal in Dumaguete, take a direct bus to Sipalay (about
) or a bus to Hinoba-an (about
), and you can also transfer to a Sipalay-bound bus at Hinoba-an. Allow about
5–6 hours
, longer depending on the route taken. From Cebu, an OceanJet fast ferry to Dumaguete takes about
4 hours 30 minutes
and costs about
Sipalay is about
170km
from both Bacolod and Dumaguete. From Bacolod it takes about
4–5 hours
via the southern coastal road through Kabankalan and Hinoba-an, and from Dumaguete about
3–4 hours
. Some stretches have no streetlights after dark, so set out so that you arrive during the day.
Sipalay has its own airport in town, with a
gravel runway. AirJuan operated Cebu and Iloilo City routes from
August 2017
, but service stopped in
March 2020
, and no scheduled flights are currently confirmed, so don't include it in your itinerary.
December
through
April
is the driest period, with calm seas and good diving visibility. Monthly rainfall is lowest in February (about 37mm) and March (about 62mm), and the peak season is
February–April
November
(about 162mm) and
May
(about 190mm) are transitional months with more showers. From
June
through
October

is the rainy season, with monthly rainfall of about 240–280mm; under the influence of the southwest monsoon (Habagat), waves get high at west-facing Sipalay, and some days island hopping and boat dives are canceled.
Typhoons mostly pass through the Philippines from
July–November

; southern Negros sees less direct impact than Luzon, but indirect effects can roughen the sea for several days at a time. If you're combining this with a Negros Occidental trip, consider timing it around Bacolod's MassKara Festival in
October
or the Santo Niño festivals held in various towns around
January
Late
March
is the best time for festivals. Around the city's cityhood anniversary (
March 31
), the annual Burangoy tourism festival is held at Poblacion Beach, and in
its 12th edition took place on
March 28
. In the past, Super Typhoon Rai (Odette) struck southern Negros directly in
December 2021
, killing 16 people in Sipalay alone and damaging most accommodations, so check the forecast before departing at year's end as well.

Accommodation is concentrated mainly in two areas, Sugar Beach and Punta Ballo. Along Sugar Beach, simple wooden bungalows and guesthouses line the shore, where you can get a beachfront room for around

a night, and there are also distinctive places like the long-running Takatuka Lodge. Punta Ballo is mostly dive resorts, so bundling with a diving package is economical, and mid-range resorts run about
. There are cheap lodges in town, but since they're away from the beach, they're not recommended.

Most meals are eaten at restaurants attached to your accommodation. Grilled fish caught daily, kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar), calamares, and crab dishes are common, and since many places are run by Europeans, pizza and pasta are also easy to find. Chicken inasal (charcoal-grilled chicken), a Negros specialty, can be enjoyed cheaply at restaurants in town. When passing through Bacolod, piaya and other Bacolod snacks make good souvenirs.
Punta Ballo has a cluster of dive resorts, including Artistic Diving Resort, opened by a Swiss instructor in

, and Easy Diving, a PADI 5-star center, so you can ask about packages combining a room and diving. Poblacion Beach in town is a light brown sand beach about 1.9 km long with good sunsets, and the food park and public market next to it serve inexpensive grilled dishes and seafood.
There are ATMs in Sipalay town, but they're often out of order or out of cash. Withdraw enough cash for your whole trip in Bacolod beforehand.
Many small Sugar Beach accommodations don't accept card payments, and electricity and internet can be unstable.
Early morning buses are less crowded and less likely to be delayed by roadwork. If you depart in the afternoon, you may arrive after dark.
How the bangka to Sugar Beach operates changes with the tide, so let your accommodation know your arrival time in advance.
Bring reef-safe sunscreen, since it's hard to find locally — prepare it in advance.
Mosquitoes are plentiful, so bring repellent and long clothing. Also check whether your bungalow has a mosquito net.
For sunset photos, shoot from the rocks at the north end of Sugar Beach, framing bangkas and palm trees together.
If you're planning a loop around Negros, the efficient route is from Sipalay south through Hinoba-an and Bais to Dumaguete.
After diving, wait at least
18 hours
before flying, as a general rule. Avoid diving the day before your flight home.
Small accommodations at Sugar Beach fill up early during peak season (
February–April
) and on weekends, so book ahead.
During the rainy season (
June–October
), big waves roll in from the west, so if a boat tour is canceled, don't insist on going out.
The coral area off the beach has sea urchins and lionfish, so don't go in barefoot, and don't touch or step on the coral.
Sugar Beach has almost no streetlights at night and gets very dark. Bring a flashlight or headlamp.
Medical facilities are limited, so bring a basic medical kit, and check whether you have dive insurance in case of a diving accident.
There are unpaved sections and steep grades on the coastal road, so always wear a helmet when riding a motorcycle.
Kanlaon Volcano in central Negros has been erupting repeatedly since
June 2024
and, as of
September 2026
, is at Alert Level 2. Sipalay is about
110km

from the volcano, so the direct danger is small, but during eruptions ash sometimes cancels flights at Bacolod-Silay Airport or falls around Bago and Pontevedra, on the route of buses from Bacolod, so check PHIVOLCS announcements and airline notices.
Because it's remote, if transport is disrupted you may have to stay an extra day. Make sure you're back in Bacolod or Dumaguete the day before your return flight.
